Inverse of the relatedness matrix (precision matrix)

Source: R/precision.R
fastrel_inv.Rd

Computes the inverse \(A^{-1}\) of the additive relationship matrix \(A = 2\phi\) of a pedigree, i.e. the precision matrix of the additive genetic values, as a sparse matrix. It is built directly from the pedigree with the rules of Henderson (1976) and Quaas (1976), without ever computing \(A\), so it can be obtained for pedigrees far too large for fastrel_ped().

Usage

fastrel_inv(ped)

Arguments

ped

A data frame (or a tibble) with one row per individual and three columns giving the identifier of the individual, of its father and of its mother (NA or 0 if unknown). See the section Columns of ped.

Value

A symmetric sparse matrix of class "dsCMatrix" (see the package Matrix), with the identifiers of the individuals as dimnames, in the order of the rows of ped. Use as.matrix() to get a base (dense) matrix.

Details

Whereas \(A\) is dense in most pedigrees (nearly all individuals of a population end up sharing an ancestor), its inverse is always sparse: each individual adds at most six distinct entries to its upper triangle, in the cells of itself and of its parents. This is what makes the inverse useful in mixed models of genetic values (animal models), which can be fitted with \(A^{-1}\) rather than with \(A\): e.g. as covStruct=list(precision=Ainv) in spaMM::fitme() or ginverse=list(var=Ainv) in MCMCglmm::MCMCglmm().

The inverse is \(A^{-1} = \sum_i q_i q_i^\top / D_i\), where \(q_i\) has 1 for individual \(i\) and \(-1/2\) for each of its known parents, and \(D_i\) is the variance of the Mendelian sampling of \(i\), relative to the additive genetic variance: \(1/2 - (F_m + F_d)/4\) if both parents are known, \(3/4 - F_p/4\) if only parent \(p\) is known, and 1 if no parent is known, \(F\) being the inbreeding coefficients. These are computed with the algorithm of Meuwissen and Luo (1992), which needs memory proportional to the number of individuals only.

The inverse of the kinship matrix is 2 * fastrel_inv(ped). The other measures of relatedness_metrics are not offered here.

References

Henderson, C. R. (1976). A simple method for computing the inverse of a numerator relationship matrix used in prediction of breeding values. Biometrics, 32(1), 69–83. doi:10.2307/2529339

Meuwissen, T. H. E., & Luo, Z. (1992). Computing inbreeding coefficients in large populations. Genetics Selection Evolution, 24(4), 305–313. doi:10.1186/1297-9686-24-4-305

Quaas, R. L. (1976). Computing the diagonal elements and inverse of a large numerator relationship matrix. Biometrics, 32(4), 949–953. doi:10.2307/2529279

See also

fastrel_ped() for the relatedness matrix itself.

Examples

ped <- data.frame(id  = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
                  dad = c(NA,  NA,  "A", "A", "C"),
                  mom = c(NA,  NA,  "B", "B", "D"))   # E: offspring of siblings
Ainv <- fastrel_inv(ped)
Ainv
#> 5 x 5 sparse Matrix of class "dsCMatrix"
#>    A  B    C    D  E
#> A  2  1 -1.0 -1.0  .
#> B  1  2 -1.0 -1.0  .
#> C -1 -1  2.5  0.5 -1
#> D -1 -1  0.5  2.5 -1
#> E  .  . -1.0 -1.0  2

## it is the inverse of the relatedness matrix
all.equal(as.matrix(Ainv), solve(fastrel_ped(ped)))
#> [1] TRUE

## a large pedigree: the inverse is sparse
set.seed(1)
big <- sim_ped(2000)
Ainv <- fastrel_inv(big)
Matrix::nnzero(Ainv) / prod(dim(Ainv))   # share of nonzero entries
#> [1] 0.003229
